# Requester

`customer_support.obj.core.requester` · v2.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> The one human who is blocked right now. Not the buyer, not the account, and frequently neither an admin nor anyone with authority.
Three things about this person change the correct answer and only one of them is on any contact record. Their technical fluency changes it more than their seniority does: a staff engineer and a non-technical office manager reporting the identical fault need opposite replies, and getting that backwards costs either a wasted round-trip or an insulted customer. Their contact history changes it: someone who has written in three times this week is telling you something none of those tickets says on its own. And whether they are the person actually suffering changes everything downstream — the person who writes in is often reporting on behalf of someone else, which quietly breaks every reproduction attempt made against what they can tell you.
The object is deliberately about the individual and not the relationship. Everything durable and commercial — ARR, renewal, health, plan — belongs to Customer Account. What lives here is what is true of this person on this contact: what they can do, what they have already tried, how long they have waited by their own standards, and what may honestly be promised to them.


**The discriminator.** A Requester is the one human blocked right now; the Customer Account is what pays and the Named Contact is who the support plan permits to ask. A requester with no standing, no budget and no admin rights is still a Requester, and an account with nobody blocked has no Requester at all — which is why "who is the customer here" is the wrong question and "who is stuck" is the right one.


Also called: `Reporter`, `Contact`, `End User`, `Submitter`, `Caller`, `Affected User`, `The Customer`


### Questions this object answers

- Who is actually blocked, and is it the person who wrote in?
- How should this reply be pitched — what can this person actually do next, as opposed to what does their job title suggest they know?
- Are they waiting on us right now, and for how long by their own standards rather than by the queue's clock?
- Have we heard from them already this week, and does that make this a content gap rather than a ticket?
- What may be promised to this specific human, as opposed to to their employer?
- Where, in what language, and at what hour should the answer land?
- Is this contact on a trajectory toward an escalation, and is that about the fault or about our handling of it?
- Whose confirmation actually closes this — theirs, or somebody else's?


### What it is NOT responsible for

- Not what the customer is contractually owed. Entitlement owns that; a Requester only inherits it, and can be genuinely uncovered at a fully covered company.
- Not the deadline. SLA Target owns the clock, its pause condition and its calendar. This object holds only observed waiting, which is a different and coarser thing.
- Not the work. Ticket owns state, owner and clock; a Requester can have four open tickets or none and still be the same object.
- Not what was said. Conversation owns the message thread; this object owns what the thread reveals about the person.
- Not the fault. Issue owns the defect that many requesters are independently reporting.
- Not the commercial relationship. Customer Account owns ARR, renewal date and health score, and none of them may be read off this object.
- Not the account's mood. Customer Sentiment aggregates across contacts; this object holds only what this human has shown us on this thread.
- Not authority. Nothing here authorises a commercial concession, a contract change or an entitlement upgrade, however senior the asker sounds.

## States

Initial `unknown`

| State | Means | Entered when | Implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unknown` | No human resolved on this contact. More common than it should be — shared inboxes, no-reply forwards and portal submissions under a service account all land here.  | — | Nothing personal may be asserted. Fluency, history and entitlement standing are all unavailable, and any advice that depends on them should degrade rather than guess.  |
| `identified` | A specific human is attached to the contact. | `exists: thread.last_inbound` | Contact history becomes readable, and repeat contact becomes detectable at all. |
| `engaged` | They wrote last and are waiting on us. This is the state the object is named for. | `thread.ball_in_court = us` | We are the blocker. Nothing may be auto-closed, no clock may pause, and elapsed time is being charged to us whatever the declared ticket state says.  |
| `waiting_on_customer` | We answered and owe nothing until they reply. NOT a flavour of dormant: the person is still blocked, they simply owe us the next message. Collapsing the two is how a queue reports health it does not have.  | `thread.ball_in_court = them` | A chase is legitimate but must be timed to their cadence, not the queue's. This is the state in which the most tickets quietly die.  |
| `at_risk` | The contact is going badly, independent of how long it has taken. | `derived.sentiment < 0` | The problem to solve has shifted from the fault to the handling. A faster technical answer will not recover this on its own.  |
| `escalated` | Ownership has transferred with a named receiver. No entered_when, because nothing in the substrate emits escalation — this state is set by a human today and that is honest.  | — | This object stops being the driver. Escalation owns the contact, and escalation_propensity becomes a historical fact rather than a live prediction.  |
| `dormant` | Waiting on them, and long enough past it that they are probably not coming back. Distinct from resolved: the problem may still be live and simply unattended.  | `days_since(thread.last_inbound) >= 14` | The queue's most expensive false negative. The SLA clock is paused, the dashboard is green, and the customer has quietly decided we are useless.  |


## Inference patterns — 9 executable, 10 blocked


### Executable against the pipeline today

| Pattern | Kind | Reads | Yields | Statement | False positive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `req.awaiting_our_reply` | deterministic | `thread.ball_in_court = us` AND `hours_since(thread.last_inbound) >= 4` | 9000 bp | They wrote last, nobody has answered, and it has been long enough that silence is now a choice. | An automated "we've received your request" acknowledgement counted as our reply by the connector, flipping ball_in_court to `them` and back on the next inbound — so the four hours are measured from the wrong message. Equally: a customer answered by phone or in a chat widget looks like continuing silence to a mail-derived signal, and this fires on a thread where somebody has already spoken to them.  |
| `req.past_their_own_reply_cadence` | deterministic | `thread.ball_in_court = them` AND `hours_since(thread.last_inbound) > {'baseline': 'reply_cadence', 'mult': 2, 'floor': 48}` | 8000 bp → `response_latency` | We are waiting on them and they have gone well past their own learned reply rhythm. | Annual leave, illness and a public holiday in their country all look identical to this. So does a requester who took our last answer, tried it, and is testing it for a week — which is the single most common cause and the one where a chase reads as nagging.  |
| `req.abandoned_the_thread` | deterministic | `thread.ball_in_court = them` AND `days_since(thread.last_inbound) >= 14` AND `derived.engagement <= 0.5` | 8500 bp → `response_latency` | Waiting on them, a fortnight of silence, and two-way volume has halved — they are not coming back. | A customer who solved it themselves produces an identical trace to a customer who gave up on us, and the two want opposite responses. Also fires on seasonal shutdowns and on requesters who moved the conversation to a channel we do not ingest — a Slack Connect channel or a phone call to their account manager.  |
| `req.freshly_blocked_relative_to_their_rhythm` | heuristic | `thread.ball_in_court = us` AND `hours_since(thread.last_inbound) <= {'baseline': 'reply_cadence', 'mult': 0.25, 'floor': 2}` | 6500 bp | Their message is very recent measured against their own rhythm, and we have not answered — this is a live block, not an archived complaint. | A person hammering us four times in an hour and a person who sent one calm note are indistinguishable to it — the engine cannot count messages inside a window — and those two want opposite responses. It also fires on a courtesy "thanks, that worked", where the ball is technically ours and nothing at all is blocked.  |
| `req.repeat_contact_by_graph_degree` | heuristic | `edge_count >= 4` AND `derived.engagement >= 1.5` | 5500 bp | This requester is attached to an unusually busy graph while two-way volume is climbing — they are probably back for the same thing. | A requester at a densely-modelled enterprise account inflates edge_count without contacting us at all, and a requester whose three genuine contacts landed in three unconnected threads deflates it to nothing. It is therefore biased toward large accounts and blind to exactly the small ones where repeat contact predicts churn.  |
| `req.unhappy_and_waiting_on_us` | heuristic | `derived.sentiment < 0` AND `thread.ball_in_court = us` | 6000 bp → `escalation_propensity` | Observation balance has gone negative while the next move is ours. | A perfectly calm requester who mentions a competitor's product, or who is describing a severe fault in vivid language while being entirely happy with us, both score negative. The mirror miss is worse: the polite chaser on their third "any update on this?" scores neutral and is the one who escalates without warning.  |
| `req.broken_promise_to_this_human` | heuristic | `thread.ball_in_court = us` AND `hours_since(commitment.due_at) > 0` | 7000 bp → `escalation_propensity` | We owe them the next message and a commitment made on this thread is already past due. | commitment.due_at is thread-scoped, not person-scoped, so a promise made to a different participant on the same thread fires it against this requester. It also cannot see a promise that was kept by phone or in a channel we do not ingest, so an agent who called the customer on Tuesday as agreed is recorded as having broken the promise.  |
| `req.call_happened_and_nothing_was_written` | heuristic | `meeting.status = completed` AND `no_obs: followup_sent` | 7500 bp → `escalation_propensity` | A meeting with this requester completed and no follow-up has been sent since. | A recurring team standup attached to the same graph node fires this every week. The literal `completed` is pack-defined: if the shipped pack emits `held` or `done` instead, this pattern silently never fires at all, which is the more dangerous failure because nobody sees a zero.  |
| `req.proxy_reporter_suspected` | heuristic | `has_obs: introduction` AND `edge_count >= 2` | 5000 bp → `is_affected_user` | An introduction was made on this thread and the requester sits between more than one party — they may be reporting on someone else's behalf. | The `introduction` observation was trained on sales handoffs. On a support thread it fires equally on "looping in Dev, who is the one actually seeing this" and on "adding our new account manager", and it cannot tell an introduction OF the affected user from an introduction TO anybody else. It will also miss the commonest proxy of all — the office manager who never introduces anyone and simply relays.  |


### Blocked — needs a signal the pipeline does not emit

| Pattern | Kind | Needs | Would yield | Statement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `req.named_contact_on_the_plan` | deterministic | `entitlement.plan` (fact_path), `entitlement_checked` (obs_kind) | 9500 bp | This specific human is listed as a covered contact on the account's support plan. |
| `req.is_the_account_admin` | deterministic | `account.contact_role` (fact_path) | 9000 bp | The contact record marks this person as an administrator on the account. |
| `req.repeat_contact_inside_a_week` | deterministic | `derived.contact_frequency` (derived), `contact_rate_per_account` (baseline) | 9000 bp | This person has contacted us several times inside a short window. |
| `req.shared_mailbox_is_not_a_person` | deterministic | `conversation.from_address` (fact_path), `ticket.channel` (fact_path) | 9000 bp | The contact arrived from a role address rather than an individual, so no personal attribute on this object is safe to assert. |
| `req.fluency_from_what_they_attach` | heuristic | `diagnostic_artifact_attached` (obs_kind), `reproduction_confirmed` (obs_kind) | 8500 bp | A requester who pastes a stack trace, a HAR file or a config diff unprompted is fluent, whatever their title says. |
| `req.read_the_docs_before_writing_in` | heuristic | `self_service_attempted` (obs_kind), `self_service_abandoned` (obs_kind) | 8000 bp | They searched the help centre, did not find it, and then wrote in — a different problem from someone who never looked. |
| `req.escalation_prone_from_history` | heuristic | `escalation_requested` (obs_kind), `derived.escalation_pressure` (fact_path) | 7000 bp | This person has escalated before, and requesters who have escalated once escalate faster the next time. |
| `req.reachable_language_and_hours` | heuristic | `conversation.language` (fact_path), `derived.requester_active_hours` (derived) | 8000 bp | Their language and their active hours can be read from the messages themselves rather than asked for. |
| `req.effort_is_high_before_they_complain` | heuristic | `ces_submitted` (obs_kind), `agent_reassigned` (obs_kind) | 7500 bp | They have re-explained, switched channel or been reassigned — the cost of getting help is already high, whatever their tone says. |
| `req.accessibility_need_declared` | heuristic | `accessibility_need_stated` (obs_kind) | 9000 bp | They have told us how a reply has to be delivered for them to be able to use it. |


## Decision factors

| Factor | Weight | Direction | Reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| technical_fluency | 2500 bp | context | `technical_fluency`, `diagnostic_capability`, `product_familiarity`, `tooling_access` |
| affected_user_certainty | 2000 bp | context | `is_affected_user`, `reports_on_behalf_of`, `affected_user_certainty_bp`, `affected_user_count` |
| contact_frequency | 1500 bp | decreases | `contact_frequency`, `open_ticket_count`, `lifetime_ticket_count`, `is_repeat_contact` |
| escalation_risk | 1500 bp | decreases | `escalation_propensity`, `effort_expressed`, `observed_sentiment`, `prior_escalation_count` |
| responsiveness | 1200 bp | increases | `response_latency`, `ball_in_court`, `engagement_trend`, `reply_cadence_hours`, `hours_waiting` |
| entitlement_standing | 700 bp | increases | `is_named_contact`, `vip_flag`, `account_ref`, `authority_scope` |
| reachability_fit | 600 bp | context | `preferred_channel`, `arrival_channel`, `language`, `timezone`, `working_hours`, `accessibility_needs` |


## Preconditions

- **`req.a_thread_exists`** At least one inbound message from this human must be visible to Layer 2. Nine of the eighteen patterns in this file read thread.last_inbound or thread.ball_in_court, and with no thread the object is a name on a form.
 _(unmet → degrade — fall back to whatever was manually entered, suppress every responsiveness inference rather than defaulting it, and mark identity_confidence_bp low. A requester with no observable thread still deserves an answer.
)_
- **`req.identity_resolves_to_one_human`** The contact must resolve to one durable human, not to a role address, a service account or a forwarded helpdesk ticket. Contact history, fluency and reply cadence are all meaningless across a rota.
 _(unmet → degrade — answer normally, but suppress contact_history and fluency inferences entirely rather than reporting them with a caveat. A caveat on a dashboard is not read; an absent number is.
)_
- **`req.account_resolved_before_entitlement_is_claimed`** account_ref must resolve before anything is said or implied about what this person is owed. An unresolved account is unknown, not free tier.
 _(unmet → degrade — hold any entitlement claim and answer the technical question meanwhile. Blocking the reply punishes the customer for our identity resolution; defaulting the entitlement downgrades a paying customer without anyone deciding to.
)_
- **`req.affected_user_question_asked_before_reproduction`** is_affected_user must be answered — not assumed — before any conclusion is drawn from a reproduction attempt, a "cannot reproduce", or a customer confirmation.
 _(unmet → block — the CONCLUSION, not the contact. Continue the conversation, keep helping, and refuse to record "no fault found" or "verified fixed" until the question has an answer. This is the single most valuable block in the file and it costs one sentence.
)_
- **`req.baseline_has_warmed_before_relative_thresholds_are_trusted`** The reply_cadence baseline must have observed enough exchanges to be a rhythm rather than a guess before response_latency is reported as anything but unknown.
 _(unmet → degrade — every relative pattern in this file already carries a floor, and a cold-start baseline resolves to that floor. The floors are the fallback, so the system remains correct and becomes merely conservative, which is the right failure direction for chasing a human.
)_
- **`req.personal_data_is_in_scope_for_this_use`** Attributes marked confidential — display_name, accessibility_needs, prior_csat_mean, prior_escalation_count, seniority_band, observed_sentiment, vip_flag, response_latency, working_hours — may only be resolved into a compile whose audience is no wider than the audience of the evidence they came from.
 _(unmet → block — the attribute, not the object. Rule 10 is not a preference, and the failure mode is not hypothetical: an accessibility need disclosed in a private ticket appearing in an account-level summary is a disclosure the customer did not make.
)_


## Constraints

- **`req.entitlement_belongs_to_the_account`** A requester cannot hold entitlement personally; it is inherited from the account and may be limited to named contacts.
- **`req.cannot_promise_beyond_entitlement`** Nothing may be committed to this requester that exceeds what the account's entitlement allows, however reasonable the request or senior the asker.
- **`req.proxy_cannot_verify_resolution`** A requester with is_affected_user false cannot provide the confirmation that closes a contact.
- **`req.no_chase_outside_their_hours`** Automated chases must respect working_hours and timezone where known. A 3am nudge is a complaint we generated ourselves. _(soft)_
- **`req.no_auto_close_while_ball_is_ours`** A contact may never be auto-closed for inactivity while ball_in_court is us. Our silence is not their disengagement.
- **`req.fluency_is_never_inferred_from_title`** role_title, seniority_band and is_admin may not be used as sources for technical_fluency, diagnostic_capability or authority_scope.
- **`req.arrival_channel_is_not_severity`** The channel a contact arrived on may set the customer's expectation of latency. It may not set severity, and may set priority only through an entitlement that genuinely differentiates channels.
- **`req.history_may_not_lower_service_level`** prior_escalation_count, prior_csat_mean and escalation history may inform how a contact is handled. They may never route a requester to a slower queue or a lower tier.


## Business rules

- **`req.proxy_cannot_close_the_reproduction`** When is_affected_user is false, a failed reproduction recorded against this requester's account may not be treated as evidence that the fault does not exist. The proxy answered a question about someone else's screen.
 — _"Cannot reproduce" closed against a proxy is the most expensive wrong conclusion in diagnosis, because it stops the investigation AND tells the customer they imagined it.
_
- **`req.no_diagnostics_beyond_capability`** Instructions requiring log collection, developer tools or configuration access must not be sent to a requester whose diagnostic_capability is cannot_gather or whose technical_fluency is none or basic, unless a no-capability fallback is offered alongside.
 — _Three failed instruction rounds are slower than one screen-share, and each failed round teaches the customer that we do not understand their situation.
_
- **`req.admin_is_not_authority`** is_admin true grants product permissions and nothing else. An admin's request is never a contractual instruction and never an entitlement upgrade, no matter how senior they sound.
 — _The admin flag is inherited from provisioning. Reading it as authority is how a support conversation quietly becomes a commercial commitment nobody was authorised to make.
_
- **`req.no_auto_close_inside_their_own_cadence`** A contact must not be auto-closed for inactivity while the ball is with the requester and the elapsed time is still inside twice their learned reply cadence. Closing a slow-but- consistent requester on a queue-wide clock is a metric improvement and a service failure.
 — _Auto-close exists to skip the chase. The chase is the step that separates a fixed problem from an abandoned one, which is why auto-closed tickets are the ones that reopen.
_
- **`req.repeat_contact_is_our_defect`** A requester contacting us repeatedly in a short window raises a content-gap or product flag regardless of whether each individual contact was resolved cleanly. Four clean resolutions to the same person in a week is four failures to solve it once.
 — _First contact resolution is the operational metric most tightly correlated with satisfaction — roughly one point of CSAT per point of FCR — and repeat contact is what its absence looks like from the customer's side. Routed to content and product, never to agent review.
_
- **`req.reply_in_their_language`** A reply must be composed in the requester's language when known. Machine translation of a diagnostic instruction is a correctness risk and not merely a tone one.
 — _The customer carries the risk of the mistranslation and we take the credit for the fast reply. Diagnostic imperatives are the highest-risk sentences in support to translate badly, because a mistranslated instruction changes what the customer actually does to their system.
_
- **`req.unnamed_contact_is_not_uncovered_customer`** is_named_contact false must never be used to refuse help outright before the account entitlement has been checked. It bounds what may be promised, not whether to answer.
 — _Named-contact lists are written at contract signature and never revisited. Refusing on a stale list refuses the right person for the wrong reason, in front of an audience that includes their employer.
_
- **`req.accessibility_needs_persist`** Once accessibility_needs is populated, every subsequent reply on any channel must honour it without the requester restating it.
 — _Re-asking is the failure. A customer who has to negotiate access to help on every contact stops contacting, and that shows up in the metrics as an improvement.
_


## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **A three-word reply, a missing greeting and a bare imperative from a requester writing in a second language are EFFORT, not contempt. Many languages mark politeness with mood or particles that do not survive translation, and English imperatives read as brusque to English speakers and as neutral to almost everyone else. Read register against language, or do not read it.
** — Every sentiment and tone model in support was trained on native-speaker register. Applying it across a language boundary systematically scores non-native speakers as angrier, which routes them to de-escalation they did not need and away from the technical answer they did — and it does so most reliably to the customers already having the hardest time getting help.
 _(overrides req.unhappy_and_waiting_on_us, req.reply_in_their_language)_
- **High contact frequency during onboarding, migration, implementation or the first weeks after a major release is the product working as sold, not a defect signal. Flagging it teaches the account to stop asking, which is the exact outcome the metric was invented to prevent.
** — Repeat contact is a defect signal only against a stable baseline. During a change window there is no baseline, and the accounts that contact most are the accounts adopting fastest. Suppress the flag for the window; do not suppress the content capture, because these are the contacts that write the best articles.
 _(overrides req.repeat_contact_is_our_defect, req.repeat_contact_inside_a_week, req.repeat_contact_by_graph_degree)_
- **A requester with expert technical_fluency and cannot_gather diagnostic_capability is a normal and specific case, not a contradiction to be resolved. The correct response is neither to send them beginner instructions nor to keep asking for artefacts they are not permitted to produce — it is to ask them what they CAN see and reason with them at their level about it.
** — Managed devices, regulated environments and locked-down enterprise laptops are the default in exactly the accounts that pay most. The rule that gates diagnostics on fluency is a shorthand; the real gate is capability, and treating a locked-down expert as a novice loses the best diagnostic partner on the ticket.
 _(overrides req.no_diagnostics_beyond_capability, req.fluency_from_what_they_attach)_
- **In mediated accounts — a security policy that forbids vendor contact with end users, a managed service provider, a clinical or classified environment — the proxy IS the contract, and routing around them to reach the affected user is a policy breach on the customer's side. The right move is to instrument the proxy, not to bypass them.
** — The proxy rules in this file assume that reaching the sufferer is merely inconvenient. Where it is prohibited, insisting on it stalls the ticket indefinitely and looks to the customer like we do not understand their environment. Verification still degrades — script the steps, ask for output verbatim, and record the closure as proxy-verified rather than customer-verified so the reduced confidence survives into the metrics.
 _(overrides req.proxy_cannot_verify_resolution, req.proxy_cannot_close_the_reproduction, req.ask_who_is_affected)_
- **Several prior escalations that all trace to a single major incident are ONE event, not a disposition. Counting them as history manufactures a difficult-customer label out of a week when we were the difficult party.
** — prior_escalation_count has no notion of correlation. A customer who escalated three times during a four-day outage behaves identically in the data to a customer who escalates on every third ticket, and the two want opposite handling — the first wants an apology and normal service, the second wants a different engagement model.
 _(overrides req.escalation_prone_from_history)_
- **During a live customer-impacting incident, the working-hours and preferred-channel constraints yield. A requester whose production is down wants the 3am message, and withholding it to respect their calendar is a courtesy they did not ask for.
** — The quiet-hours rule optimises for not manufacturing complaints out of routine nudges. It was never meant to govern incident communication, where the complaint is generated by silence instead. The test is blast radius, not the requester's tone: a SEV1 or SEV2 overrides, a SEV3 with a workaround does not.
 _(overrides req.no_chase_outside_their_hours, req.confirm_channel_and_language)_
- **Some VIP flags encode a genuine executive-sponsor or named-contact clause rather than office politics. The correct response to a VIP flag is to verify what it encodes, not to strip it.
** — The rule treating vip_flag as political is right about most of them and wrong about the ones that were negotiated. Stripping a contractual flag because the field has a bad reputation breaches an agreement, and it does so invisibly because the agreement lives in a contract nobody in the queue has read.
 _(overrides req.history_may_not_lower_service_level)_
- **Baseline-relative chasing is right for hygiene and wrong when a contractual or regulatory clock is running against the customer's own reply. If their silence will cost them an entitlement, a warranty window or a legal deadline, chase on the deadline's schedule, not on theirs.
** — Every relative-cadence rule in this file optimises for not nagging. That trade is correct when the only cost of waiting is our metric, and inverted when the cost of waiting is theirs. This is also the one exception where a business-hours SLA calendar matters more than the requester's own hours, because the calendar is what the deadline is measured against.
 _(overrides req.no_auto_close_inside_their_own_cadence, req.chase_on_their_cadence, req.past_their_own_reply_cadence)_


## Best practices

- **Ask who is actually seeing the problem in the first reply, before writing a single reproduction step.** — A wrong guess costs one sentence; a missed proxy costs the entire reproduction attempt and two days, and it ends in a "cannot reproduce" that tells the customer they imagined it. It is the highest return-on-effort question in support and the most skipped, because the answer feels obvious and is not.

- **Infer technical fluency from what they wrote and attached, never from their title or their admin flag.** — Title is wrong in both directions and confidently so. The first message routinely contains a stack trace, a config diff or a precise description of an intermittent race condition — all stronger evidence of capability than any field on the contact record, and all currently discarded by the pipeline.

- **Time every chase to this person's own reply cadence rather than to a queue-wide interval.** — A requester who always takes three days is consistent, not slow. Chasing them at twenty-four hours trains them to filter our follow-ups, after which the one chase that actually mattered is filtered too. The cost of the rule is that it makes the queue's aggregate look slower.

- **When a contact becomes an article, a macro or a content-gap ticket, capture the requester's own phrasing rather than translating it into internal vocabulary.** — The customer's words are the search terms of the next customer. Rewriting into product-internal naming is precisely how a correct article becomes unfindable, and it is the failure that makes a knowledge base look well-stocked and useless. This is KCS doctrine and it is doctrine because everyone gets it wrong the first time.

- **Send the diagnostic ask and the zero-capability alternative in the same message.** — Probing for capability first costs a round-trip and reads as a test. Offering both lets the requester self-select in one exchange, and it is the only version of the interaction where a cannot_gather requester does not feel like an obstacle to their own support ticket.

- **Send repeat contact to content-gap analysis and product feedback before it reaches any agent scorecard.** — Four clean resolutions to one person in a week is four failures to solve it once, and none of them is the agent's. Routing it to quality assurance produces defensiveness and better ticket notes; routing it to content produces an article and a smaller queue.

- **Confirm channel, language, timezone, working hours and access needs once, and carry them across every subsequent contact and channel.** — Each of these is cheap to ask and expensive to re-ask. An accessibility need restated on every contact is a customer negotiating access to help repeatedly, and the customers who stop negotiating show up in the metrics as an improvement.

- **Take resolution confirmation from the person who was broken, not from the person who reported it.** — Verification is the step that separates a fixed problem from an abandoned one, and it is almost always skipped. A proxy's "they say it's fine now" is the most common precursor to a reopen, and a reopen after a claimed verification is a worse finding than never closing.

- **Set pace from impact and how fast the damage is growing; set tone from the person. Never let the emotional register of the message set the queue position.** — Priority is impact multiplied by urgency, and neither term is "how upset the writer sounds". A queue that responds to volume teaches every customer that escalating language is the way to get served, and the quiet ones — who are frequently the worst affected — learn it last.



## Anti-patterns

- **Treating a senior job title as evidence of technical capability, decision authority or entitlement.** — tempting because The title is the only field on the contact record that looks like it means something, and in most other business contexts it does. A VP genuinely can approve things — just not the things support needs approved, and not on their own product estate.
 Instead: Read capability from the message and authority from the contract. Keep role_title for tone and for nothing else, which is what the constraint in this file enforces.

- **Directing every question, instruction and verification at whoever wrote in, without ever establishing whether they are the person experiencing the fault.** — tempting because The writer is the only person in the thread. Every ticketing system defaults is_affected_user to true, the reply-to address is right there, and asking "who is actually seeing this?" feels like a stalling question when the customer is already waiting.
 Instead: Ask once, in the first reply, in one sentence. Where the sufferer cannot be reached, instrument the proxy with an exact script and record the closure as proxy-verified.

- **Letting the emotional register of the message set the response speed and the queue position.** — tempting because It feels like empathy, it is immediately rewarded — the angry customer stops being angry — and the calm customer never complains about being deprioritised, so the feedback loop only ever points one way.
 Instead: Set pace from impact and how fast the damage is growing, and tone from the person. Both can be high; they are separate dials, and priority is the product of impact and urgency, not of volume.

- **Reading a short, greeting-less, imperative message from a non-native speaker as hostility, and routing it to de-escalation instead of to an answer.** — tempting because Every sentiment and tone model in support was trained on native-speaker register, and a human agent under load applies the same instinct. "Send me the log now" genuinely does read as rude in English, and the agent is not wrong about the English — only about the person.
 Instead: Read register against language and language_confidence_bp. Where a language boundary exists, suppress the tone read entirely rather than discounting it — a suppressed signal is safer than a halved one.

- **Answering a contact with the help-centre article the requester has already read and found insufficient.** — tempting because It is fast, it is correct in the majority of cases, and deflection is a metric somebody is measured on. The system genuinely cannot see that they already looked, so the article is the highest-expected-value reply available to it.
 Instead: Emit self_service_attempted and self_service_abandoned and branch on them. Absent the signal, open with what the article does not cover rather than with the link.

- **Letting prior_escalation_count, prior_csat_mean or escalation history route a requester to a slower queue, a lower tier or a defensive reply template.** — tempting because The correlation is real — people who escalated once do escalate faster — so the routing rule looks like good prediction. It is usually introduced as a way to give difficult contacts to more experienced agents, which is a defensible intention.
 Instead: Use history to inform handling — brief the agent, lead with what went wrong last time — and never to lower service level. The constraint req.history_may_not_lower_service_level exists precisely to be quoted at this.

- **Treating a requester in waiting_on_customer as a resolved problem because the clock is paused and the dashboard is green.** — tempting because The pause is legitimate — we genuinely are blocked on them — and every queue metric agrees that the ticket is fine. Nothing in the operational view distinguishes a customer who is testing our fix from one who gave up a fortnight ago.
 Instead: Watch unresponsive_thread_share, not SLA attainment. Chase once on their cadence, then close with an explicit invitation rather than silently.

- **Aggregating contacts from it@ or support@ into a single requester record and then reading fluency, cadence and history off it.** — tempting because It is the default behaviour of every system that keys identity on an email address, and it produces a record that looks complete and well-populated — more complete, in fact, than most real requesters, because it accumulates everything.
 Instead: Detect the role address, set is_shared_mailbox, and suppress the personal attribute groups rather than caveating them.

- `customer_support.obj.core.conversation` — requires (hard)
- `customer_support.obj.core.ticket` — enriches (hard)
- `customer_support.obj.core.customer_account` — requires (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement` — enriches (hard)
- `customer_support.obj.core.commitment` — enriches (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.customer_sentiment` — enriches (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.support_agent` — enriches (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.escalation` — invalidated_by (soft)

## Inputs

- **email** — who wrote last and how quickly they answer
- **email** — who owes the next message
- **derived** — two-way volume against the prior fortnight
- **derived** — observation balance used as a sentiment proxy
- **derived** — promises made on this thread and their due dates
- **ticket** — channel of arrival, submitter identity, prior contact history
- **chat** — message cadence and how much the requester types before giving up
- **phone** — call outcome and whatever was verbally promised
- **help_center** — search terms and abandoned articles before the contact
- **crm** — role, admin flag, named-contact status, account link
- **survey** — how this person rated us last time and how much effort it cost them
- **telemetry** — whether the affected account actually experienced the fault
- **manual_entry** — what the agent learned by asking


## Outputs

- **`fluency_profile`** Fluency, product familiarity and what they can actually gather. Determines the shape of the reply before anything else does. → L4.reasoning_unit, L5.communication_planning
- **`affected_user_certainty_bp`** How sure we are the writer is the person experiencing the fault. Should CAP the confidence of every diagnosis built on their description rather than trigger anything. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`escalation_risk_bp`** Trajectory of this contact toward an escalation, from broken promises first, sentiment second, history third — in that order of evidential weight. → L4.decision_maker, L4.reasoning_unit
- **`repeat_contact_flag`** This person has been back. Feeds content-gap analysis, never agent performance review. → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`reachability`** Channel, language, timezone, working hours and accessibility needs as one delivery instruction. → L5.2.channel_planner
- **`expected_reply_window`** How long to wait before a chase is warranted, derived from their own cadence rather than a queue default. → L5.execution_planning
- **`entitlement_standing`** Whether this specific human is covered, and what may therefore be promised to them. Bounds the promise; never bounds the answer. → L4.decision_maker
- **`identity_confidence_bp`** How sure we are this contact is the human we think it is. Should suppress contact-history claims below roughly half, rather than caveat them. → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit


## Events

- **`req.identified`** Requester Identified
- **`req.awaiting_reply`** Requester Awaiting Reply
- **`req.went_quiet`** Requester Went Quiet — invalidates response_latency, escalation_propensity, expected_reply_by
- **`req.turned_negative`** Requester Sentiment Turned
- **`req.promise_missed`** Promise To Requester Missed — invalidates escalation_propensity
- **`req.repeat_contact_detected`** Repeat Contact Detected
- **`req.proxy_suspected`** Proxy Reporter Suspected — invalidates technical_fluency, diagnostic_capability, product_familiarity
- **`req.escalation_asked_for`** Requester Asked For Escalation — invalidates escalation_propensity


## Actions

- **Ask who is actually seeing this** (human) — One sentence, asked before any reproduction step. The highest return-on-effort question in support and the one most often skipped because the answer is assumed.

- **Match the reply to their fluency** (agent) — Rewrite the instruction up or down. Both directions are failures: jargon at a novice wastes a round-trip, hand-holding at an expert reads as contempt and costs the account's technical goodwill in one reply.

- **Offer a path that needs nothing from them** (agent) — A screen-share, a support bundle, or us reproducing it ourselves. The correct move when diagnostic_capability is cannot_gather or unknown, and it is faster than three failed instruction rounds.

- **Confirm channel, language, hours and access needs** (agent) — Asked once, reused forever. Cheap, and it stops replies landing at 3am in a language they read slowly and a format they cannot use.
- **Chase against their own baseline** (system) — One chase, timed to the person. A second automated chase inside the same window is how a requester learns to filter us, after which the one chase that mattered is also filtered.

- **Put the call in writing** (human) — Recap what was agreed and by when. Converts a remembered promise into a checkable one, which is the entire difference between a commitment and a grievance.

- **Raise this as a content gap** (agent) — For a repeat contact, in the requester's own words rather than ours — their phrasing is the search term the next requester will use. The only support action whose success is measured by work that never arrives.

- **Verify the fix with the person who was broken** (human) — Never close a proxy-reported contact on the proxy's word. "They say it's fine now" is the most common precursor to a reopen.

- **Script the steps for the relayer** (agent) — When the affected user genuinely cannot be reached — mediated accounts, security policy, shift patterns — give the proxy an exact script and ask for output verbatim rather than for a summary. Slower than talking to the sufferer and far better than a paraphrase.

- **Withhold contact history from this compile** (system) — Applied when identity confidence is low or the contact is a shared mailbox. Suppress rather than caveat: a caveat on a dashboard is not read, and a fictional history is worse than none.



## Evidence

- **telemetry** · 9000 bp — The affected session itself. The only source that settles the proxy question without asking, and it outranks anything the requester says about it. Decays because a session from last month proves the fault existed, not that it exists.

- **ticket** · 8000 bp — Submitter identity and prior contact history from the ticketing system. Strong and, today, entirely manual — the counts in contact_history have no automated source at all.
- **crm** · 7500 bp — Role, admin flag, named-contact status. Strong for standing and worthless for fluency; someone typed it once and never revisited it, which is exactly why it decays fastest of anything on this list.

- **manual_entry** · 7000 bp — What the agent learned by asking. Honest, unverifiable, written by the person being measured — and today the only source for technical_fluency, diagnostic_capability and accessibility_needs, which are the three fields that most change the answer.

- **email** · 7000 bp — What they wrote and how they wrote it. The richest fluency evidence available and the least structured. Not independent of derived, which is computed from it.
- **chat** · 6500 bp — Cadence and abandonment. Reveals frustration earlier than email because there is no time to soften it — and absence of a reply proves less here than in email, because chats are abandoned mid-sentence routinely. Sustained abandonment above roughly 8% is a queue problem, not a customer one.

- **phone** · 6000 bp — High information, near-zero retention. Whatever was promised on a call exists only in the customer's memory unless someone writes it down.
- **survey** · 5000 bp — Their prior rating of us. Genuine, and answered almost entirely by the delighted and the furious — the satisfied middle is invisible, so a mean of two responses is a mood rather than a measurement.

- **help_center** · 4500 bp — Search and abandonment behaviour before the contact. Circumstantial about the person, precise about the content gap.
- **derived** · 4000 bp — Engagement and sentiment shapes. Corroborating only, and explicitly independent of NOTHING — it is computed from the same correspondence as email and chat, so it must never be counted as a second opinion on them.



## Metrics

- **proxy_detection_rate** (percent) — Share of proxy-reported contacts identified before the first reproduction attempt rather than after it failed. The metric this object exists to move.
- **fluency_classification_accuracy** (percent) — Share of inferred fluency levels an agent later agreed with. Calibrates the highest-weighted decision factor on this object; if it cannot be measured, the weight is a guess.
- **first_contact_resolution_by_fluency** (percent) — FCR split by fluency band. Published benchmarks put good FCR around 70–79%, with roughly a one-to-one relationship between FCR points and CSAT points — so if the bands do not differ, the fluency inference is not doing any work and should be treated as unproven.

- **repeat_contact_rate** (percent) — Share of requesters contacting more than once inside a week. A product and content metric wearing a support badge; routed to content-gap analysis, never to agent review.
- **requester_reply_latency** (hours) — Observed time for this person to answer us. Feeds the reply_cadence baseline rather than a queue average. Deliberately carries no direction — it is a description of a human, not a target for us, and treating it as one is how chase schedules become nagging.

- **unresponsive_thread_share** (percent) — Share of open contacts parked on the requester past twice their own cadence. The queue's hidden backlog, and the only number that makes a paused clock visible.
- **chat_abandonment_share** (percent) — Share of chats this requester population abandons before an answer. Healthy contact centres sit around 2–5%; sustained figures above 8% indicate a staffing or routing failure. Recorded here because an abandonment is counted as a deflection success by every deflection metric, which is why deflection must never be read as first-contact resolution.

- **requester_effort_score** (score) — How hard it was for this person to get resolved. Kept alongside satisfaction because low effort predicts retention more reliably than delight does — a calm customer who re-explained three times is a churn risk no sentiment score will show.

- **channel_preference_hit_rate** (percent) — Share of replies delivered on the requester's stated preferred channel, in their language, inside their working hours.
- **accessibility_restatement_rate** (percent) — Share of contacts on which a requester had to restate an accessibility need we already held. Should be zero; is not.

## Examples

- **Office manager reporting for a developer** _(typical)_ — is_affected_user false, technical_fluency basic, diagnostic_capability cannot_gather. Every reproduction question is answered by someone relaying an answer, and the thread reads as an unreproducible bug for two days before anyone asks who is actually seeing it.

- **Staff engineer at a customer, pastes a stack trace in the first message** _(typical)_ — technical_fluency expert, diagnostic_capability can_reproduce_reliably. Wants the cause, not the ticket number. Sending them a getting-started article loses the account's technical goodwill in one reply, and they will not tell us why.

- **Account admin who has never used the product** _(misclassification)_ — is_admin true, technical_fluency none, is_affected_user false. Has every permission and no idea what is broken. The clearest proof that admin status and fluency are unrelated fields, and the case every title-based inference gets wrong.

- **Staff engineer on a locked-down managed laptop** _(edge)_ — technical_fluency expert, diagnostic_capability cannot_gather, tooling_access none. Looks like a contradiction and is completely ordinary in regulated accounts. Both naive responses — beginner instructions, or repeated requests for a HAR file — are wrong. See the exception req.fluent_but_locked_down.

- **it@customer.example — eleven contacts this week** _(misclassification)_ — is_shared_mailbox true and undetected. Aggregated into one fictional requester whose fluency is an average, whose reply cadence is a rota, and who trips every repeat-contact rule in the file while the organisation behaves entirely normally.

- **Fourth contact this week about the same workflow** _(typical)_ — Three tickets each closed correctly. Individually clean, collectively a content gap or a product defect. Nothing in the substrate can currently see this and it is the object's highest-value ask.

- **Fourth contact this week, in week two of a migration** _(counterexample)_ — Identical data to the row above and the opposite finding. This is the product being adopted, and flagging it as a defect signal teaches the account to stop asking. The exception req.repeat_contact_that_is_healthy exists for exactly this pair.

- **The polite chaser** _(edge)_ — Third courteous "any update on this?". derived.sentiment reads neutral throughout, escalation_propensity is genuinely high, and the gap between those two is precisely what the borrowed sentiment vocabulary cannot see. This requester escalates without warning.

- **Terse second-language requester** _(misclassification)_ — "Send log now. Not working." Scored as hostile, routed to de-escalation, and given an apology instead of an answer. The register is a translation artefact and the effort was real — this is the most common wrong read in a multilingual queue.

- **Consumer end user on a free plan** _(typical)_ — is_named_contact false, entitlement thin, escalation_propensity high because their expectations were set by consumer apps rather than by a contract. Standing bounds what may be promised, never whether to answer.

- **Requester in a language and timezone we do not staff** _(edge)_ — Every reply lands overnight and is machine-translated. Two round-trips take a working week, and the customer experiences a four-hour entitlement as four days without a single breach being recorded.

- **Enterprise contact whose security policy forbids us talking to end users** _(counterexample)_ — The proxy rules in this file say route to the sufferer. Here that is a policy breach on the customer's side, and insisting on it stalls the ticket forever. Instrument the proxy instead and record the closure as proxy-verified so the reduced confidence survives into the metrics.


## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **complete**


> All twenty-three sections authored. Fifty-four attributes across eight composite groups. Eighteen inference patterns — nine executable, nine needs_signal — and every one of them carries a false_positive, because a confidence with no stated failure case is a number nobody can argue with.
The uncomfortable summary: the system can tell you precisely how long this person has been waiting and almost nothing about what to say to them. Every attempt to infer technical_fluency, the highest-weighted decision factor on this object, is in the needs_signal list. Everything that fires today fires off thread.*, commitment.*, meeting.*, derived.* and graph degree.
The four asks that would change this object most, in order: (1) conversation.from_address — the cheapest signal in the backlog and the one whose absence corrupts the most fields, because without it a role mailbox is silently modelled as a person; (2) derived.contact_frequency — turns three unremarkable tickets into one alarming pattern and retires the graph-degree heuristic that currently stands in for it; (3) diagnostic_artifact_attached — the best evidence of fluency there is, arriving unasked in the first message and discarded; (4) escalation_requested — there is no escalation signal of any kind in the substrate, so the loudest thing a requester can do is inaudible.
Sensitivity is authored honestly rather than defensively. Nine attributes are confidential and each is confidential for a stated reason: they are judgements about a named individual, or data disclosed to get help rather than to be profiled. Rule 10 is enforced by the precondition req.personal_data_is_in_scope_for_this_use, which blocks the attribute and never the answer.
The section a reviewer should read first is `exceptions`. Two of the eight are marked common, which is a claim: terse non-native-speaker messages misread as rudeness, and healthy repeat contact during onboarding flagged as a defect. Both will happen this week in a queue of any size, and neither is written down in any playbook this domain has.
